newsitem.title: Peru: Angry silence marks month of Peru hostage drama.
newsitem.headline: Angry silence marks month of Peru hostage drama.

text.p: Peru's government and Marxist rebels marked a month of the hostage crisis in angry deadlock on Friday after trading mutual accustions over failure to make progress in the standoff.

The Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA), holding 74 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima, vowed not to surrender without achieving the liberation of jailed comrades. It also blamed government inflexibility for prolonging the crisis.

"We have said it a million times, we will say it again. "We will never give in," Isaac Velasco, Hamburg, Germany-based international spokesman of the MRTA, said at a news conference in the Danish capital of Copenhagen.
"The crisis will end when the Peruvian government decides it will and when it is willing to make a compromise," he said.
President Alberto Fujimori's government frequently ruled out releasing MRTA prisoners but proposed setting up a peace commission to oversee talks between the two sides.
Velasco insisted the MRTA was flexible and wanted a political solution, but accused Fujimori of being "more concerned about keeping up a strong man image."
Fujimori's negotiator, Education Minister Domingo Palermo, rejected on Thursday a rebel proposal that the Guatemalan government take part in the commission.

Palermo told a news conference that trying to bring Guatemala into the talks was an effort by the rebels to suggest a false parallel between the MRTA's situation and the recently ended civil war in the Central American country where leftist guerrillas laid down arms after 30 years of fighting.
He also said Red Cross and family visits to MRTA prisoners in Peruvian jails were suspended "in order to avoid disturbing the process of talks."
Rebel leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini attempted to reply to Palermo with a statement read to reporters by walkie-talkie, but was barely intelligible due to heavy distortion.
Cerpa then used a megaphone to shout a statement.

He accused the government of creating obstacles to solving the crisis and ruled out more hostage releases anytime soon. He also called for the visits to MRTA prisoners to be resumed, saying a sign of "good will" was needed.
Late on Thursday police told about 16 photographers and TV cameramen camped on a roof opposite the residence -- the closest media vantage point -- to get down.
Local media, who have had representatives on the roof since the siege began Dec. 17, obeyed but international reporters did not immediately move and were not forced.
On Friday morning police continued tightening security at the siege site, requiring journalists to line up for accreditation and blocking all but authorised cars from passing nearby.

In Copenhagen, Velasco said MRTA wanted Spain or Italy, as well as Guatemala, to sit on the "guarantor commission" proposed by the government. Both sides agreed to the participation of the International Committee of the Red Cross and the Vatican.
The government did not say if it would accept the participation of a European country.
In a rare piece of good news for Fujimori, a major poll showed on Friday his popularity had increased significantly during the crisis.

Fujimori's approval rating rose to 50.3 percent in January from 44.9 percent in December, according to pollster Compania Peruana de Investigacion de Mercados (CPI). The poll said 65.9 percent believed Fujimori's handling of the crisis was correct, as 23.1 percent disagreed.

While many Peruvians saw much truth in the MRTA's complaints about poverty in Peru, there was general disgust at the MRTA's methods and strong support for what Fujimori called his "firm but prudent" approach to the crisis.

The poll added that an overwhelming 93.2 percent of the population believed the president should look for a peaceful solution to the siege and 88.2 percent said no rebels should be released from prison.
